_about.purpose: The world outside the text: who ruled the surrounding empires, what was happening in them, and a short background piece for each era and region.
_about.chronology: Dates follow conventional scholarly chronology, which for the Old Testament differs from the traditional chronology carried by the verse year numbers in the Theographic dataset (its creation date is -4004, i.e. Ussher). Rows are therefore joined to a verse by ERA, not by year, so a fifty-year disagreement between the two systems cannot put the wrong emperor beside the wrong verse. Years are shown as published, and the UI says which chronology it is.
_about.sources: Regnal dates compiled with reference to Wikidata (CC0) and standard reference works. Dates and names are facts and carry no licence; the note and background prose here was written for Scholia.
_about.scope: Foreign powers only. The kings of Israel and Judah are deliberately absent: they are already attached to verses as people by the Theographic dataset, and repeating them here would duplicate that.
_about.negative_years: Negative years are BC. -586 means 586 BC. There is no year zero.

rulers.name: Hammurabi
rulers.title: King of Babylon
rulers.note: Issued the law code that is the closest ancient parallel to the covenant law codes.

rulers.name: Thutmose III
rulers.title: Pharaoh of Egypt
rulers.note: Egypt's greatest conqueror; his campaigns made Canaan an Egyptian province.

rulers.name: Amenhotep II
rulers.title: Pharaoh of Egypt
rulers.note: Named by some as the pharaoh of the exodus on an early dating.

rulers.name: Akhenaten
rulers.title: Pharaoh of Egypt
rulers.note: Imposed the worship of a single sun-disc; the Amarna letters from his reign show Canaan in turmoil.

rulers.name: Ramesses II
rulers.title: Pharaoh of Egypt
rulers.note: The pharaoh of the exodus on the common later dating; builder of the store cities of the delta.

rulers.name: Merneptah
rulers.title: Pharaoh of Egypt
rulers.note: His victory stele carries the earliest known mention of Israel by name, outside the Bible.

rulers.name: Ramesses III
rulers.title: Pharaoh of Egypt
rulers.note: Fought off the Sea Peoples, among them the Peleset, whom most identify with the Philistines.

rulers.name: Ashur-rabi II
rulers.title: King of Assyria
rulers.note: Assyria at its weakest, losing territory on the Euphrates — which is precisely why a small kingdom in Canaan had room to grow.

rulers.name: Siamun
rulers.title: Pharaoh of Egypt
rulers.note: Ruled a divided, weakened Egypt; usually identified as the pharaoh whose daughter married Solomon.

rulers.name: Hiram I
rulers.title: King of Tyre
rulers.note: Supplied cedar, craftsmen and shipping for the temple and the palace, and partnered in Red Sea trade.

rulers.name: Shoshenq I
rulers.title: Pharaoh of Egypt
rulers.note: Almost certainly the Shishak who stripped the temple in Rehoboam's fifth year.

rulers.name: Taharqa
rulers.title: Pharaoh of Egypt
rulers.note: The Cushite pharaoh whose approach drew Sennacherib away from Jerusalem.

rulers.name: Necho II
rulers.title: Pharaoh of Egypt
rulers.note: Killed Josiah at Megiddo, then lost the east to Babylon at Carchemish.

rulers.name: Apries (Hophra)
rulers.title: Pharaoh of Egypt
rulers.note: The Egyptian ally whose relief force failed to save Jerusalem.

rulers.name: Tiglath-Pileser III
rulers.title: King of Assyria
rulers.note: Rebuilt Assyria into an empire of provinces and deportations; the Pul of 2 Kings.

rulers.name: Shalmaneser V
rulers.title: King of Assyria
rulers.note: Besieged Samaria for three years.

rulers.name: Sargon II
rulers.title: King of Assyria
rulers.note: Claims the capture of Samaria and the deportation of its people.

rulers.name: Sennacherib
rulers.title: King of Assyria
rulers.note: Took forty-six towns of Judah and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage', but did not take the city.

rulers.name: Esarhaddon
rulers.title: King of Assyria
rulers.note: Conquered Egypt, bringing Assyria to its greatest extent.

rulers.name: Ashurbanipal
rulers.title: King of Assyria
rulers.note: Assembled the great library at Nineveh; after him Assyria collapsed within a generation.

rulers.name: Nabopolassar
rulers.title: King of Babylon
rulers.note: Broke Assyria with Median help and founded the Neo-Babylonian empire.

rulers.name: Nebuchadnezzar II
rulers.title: King of Babylon
rulers.note: Deported Judah in stages and destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in 586.

rulers.name: Amel-Marduk (Evil-Merodach)
rulers.title: King of Babylon
rulers.note: Released Jehoiachin from prison and gave him a seat at the royal table.

rulers.name: Nabonidus
rulers.title: King of Babylon
rulers.note: Spent years at Teima leaving his son Belshazzar in Babylon; the last Babylonian king.

rulers.name: Cyrus the Great
rulers.title: King of Persia
rulers.note: Took Babylon in 539 and let deported peoples return home and rebuild their temples.

rulers.name: Cambyses II
rulers.title: King of Persia
rulers.note: Added Egypt to the Persian empire.

rulers.name: Darius I
rulers.title: King of Persia
rulers.note: Confirmed Cyrus's decree and funded the finishing of the second temple.

rulers.name: Xerxes I (Ahasuerus)
rulers.title: King of Persia
rulers.note: The Ahasuerus of Esther; invaded Greece and lost at Salamis.

rulers.name: Artaxerxes I
rulers.title: King of Persia
rulers.note: Sent Ezra, and later Nehemiah, to Jerusalem.

rulers.name: Darius III
rulers.title: King of Persia
rulers.note: Lost the empire to Alexander.

rulers.name: Alexander the Great
rulers.title: King of Macedon
rulers.note: Conquered the Persian empire in a decade and made Greek the language of the eastern Mediterranean.

rulers.name: Ptolemy I Soter
rulers.title: King of Egypt
rulers.note: Founded the dynasty that ruled Judea for a century.

rulers.name: Ptolemy II Philadelphus
rulers.title: King of Egypt
rulers.note: Tradition credits his library with commissioning the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament.

rulers.name: Antiochus III the Great
rulers.title: Seleucid King
rulers.note: Took Judea from the Ptolemies in 198, then lost the west to Rome.

rulers.name: Antiochus IV Epiphanes
rulers.title: Seleucid King
rulers.note: Outlawed the Jewish law and desecrated the temple, provoking the Maccabean revolt.

rulers.name: Judas Maccabeus
rulers.title: Leader of the Jewish revolt
rulers.note: Retook Jerusalem and rededicated the temple, the origin of Hanukkah.

rulers.name: John Hyrcanus
rulers.title: Hasmonean ruler and high priest
rulers.note: Expanded an independent Jewish state and forcibly converted the Idumeans, Herod's people.

rulers.name: Alexander Jannaeus
rulers.title: Hasmonean king
rulers.note: His reign hardened the split between Pharisees and Sadducees.

rulers.name: Pompey the Great
rulers.title: Roman general
rulers.note: Took Jerusalem in 63 BC and walked into the holy of holies; Judea became a Roman client.

rulers.name: Julius Caesar
rulers.title: Dictator of Rome
rulers.note: Granted the Jews protected status for their religion, a privilege that outlasted him.

rulers.name: Herod the Great
rulers.title: King of Judea
rulers.note: Roman client king and vast builder; rebuilt the temple. The king of the nativity narrative.

rulers.name: Augustus
rulers.title: Emperor of Rome
rulers.note: First emperor; the census decree of Luke 2 is issued in his name.

rulers.name: Herod Archelaus
rulers.title: Ethnarch of Judea
rulers.note: So brutal that Rome deposed him and took Judea under direct rule.

rulers.name: Herod Antipas
rulers.title: Tetrarch of Galilee and Perea
rulers.note: Ruled Jesus' home region; executed John the Baptist.

rulers.name: Herod Philip II
rulers.title: Tetrarch of Iturea and Trachonitis
rulers.note: Rebuilt Caesarea Philippi, where Peter made his confession.

rulers.name: Annas
rulers.title: High Priest
rulers.note: Deposed by Rome but still called high priest; five of his sons and his son-in-law held the office after him.

rulers.name: Tiberius
rulers.title: Emperor of Rome
rulers.note: Emperor through the whole public ministry; the coin of the tribute question bore his head.

rulers.name: Caiaphas
rulers.title: High Priest
rulers.note: Son-in-law of Annas; presided at the trial of Jesus. His ossuary was found in Jerusalem in 1990.

rulers.name: Pontius Pilate
rulers.title: Prefect of Judea
rulers.note: Held the sole power of execution in Judea. Named in an inscription found at Caesarea in 1961.

rulers.name: Caligula
rulers.title: Emperor of Rome
rulers.note: Ordered his statue erected in the temple; only his assassination stopped it.

rulers.name: Herod Agrippa I
rulers.title: King of Judea
rulers.note: Killed James and imprisoned Peter; died suddenly at Caesarea.

rulers.name: Claudius
rulers.title: Emperor of Rome
rulers.note: Expelled the Jews from Rome around AD 49, which is how Paul met Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth.

rulers.name: Herod Agrippa II
rulers.title: King of Chalcis
rulers.note: The Agrippa before whom Paul made his defence at Caesarea.

rulers.name: Nero
rulers.title: Emperor of Rome
rulers.note: The Caesar to whom Paul appealed; blamed the fire of Rome on Christians and began the first imperial persecution.

rulers.name: Antonius Felix
rulers.title: Procurator of Judea
rulers.note: Kept Paul in custody at Caesarea for two years hoping for a bribe.

rulers.name: Porcius Festus
rulers.title: Procurator of Judea
rulers.note: Heard Paul's appeal to Caesar and sent him to Rome.

rulers.name: Vespasian
rulers.title: Emperor of Rome
rulers.note: Commanded the war in Judea before becoming emperor in the year of four emperors.

rulers.name: Titus
rulers.title: Emperor of Rome
rulers.note: Destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70; his arch in Rome shows the temple treasures carried away.

rulers.name: Domitian
rulers.title: Emperor of Rome
rulers.note: Demanded divine honours; the traditional setting for the exile on Patmos and Revelation.

rulers.name: Trajan
rulers.title: Emperor of Rome
rulers.note: His correspondence with Pliny is the earliest outside account of how Rome handled Christians.

events.title: The Code of Hammurabi
events.summary: Babylon publishes a law code on a stone stele. Its case-law form, and several of its provisions, run strikingly close to the covenant laws of Exodus.

events.title: The Amarna letters
events.summary: Canaanite city-kings write to Egypt begging for troops against raiders they call the Habiru. The letters show a Canaan of small quarrelling city-states under weakening Egyptian control.

events.title: The Merneptah stele names Israel
events.summary: An Egyptian victory monument lists 'Israel' among defeated peoples in Canaan — the earliest mention of Israel anywhere outside the Bible.

events.title: The Sea Peoples invade
events.summary: A wave of migrating peoples brings down the Hittite empire and is fought off by Egypt. One group, the Peleset, settles the coast of Canaan and becomes the Philistines of Judges and Samuel.

events.title: The Bronze Age collapse
events.summary: Empires and trade networks fail across the eastern Mediterranean. The resulting power vacuum is what allows small highland peoples, Israel among them, to establish themselves.

events.title: Egypt fragments
events.summary: Egypt splits between pharaohs in the north and the high priests of Amun in the south, ending its control of Canaan. For roughly a century no great power holds the Levant.

events.title: Phoenicia turns to the sea
events.summary: Tyre and Sidon build a maritime trading network across the Mediterranean. Their timber, metalwork and shipping are what made Solomon's building programme and Red Sea ventures possible.

events.title: Shishak's campaign into Judah
events.summary: Pharaoh Shoshenq I raids Judah and Israel five years after the kingdom splits, stripping the temple treasury. His own list of captured towns survives at Karnak.

events.title: The Battle of Qarqar
events.summary: Assyria fights a coalition of Levantine kings. The Assyrian account names 'Ahab the Israelite' with two thousand chariots — the first appearance of an Israelite king in a foreign record.

events.title: Jehu pays tribute to Assyria
events.summary: The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III shows an Israelite king bowing before the Assyrian — the only likely contemporary portrait of a biblical monarch.

events.title: The fall of Samaria
events.summary: After a three-year siege Assyria takes Samaria and deports the northern kingdom. Israel as a state ends; only Judah is left.

events.title: Sennacherib invades Judah
events.summary: Assyria takes forty-six walled towns of Judah and besieges Jerusalem. Sennacherib's own annals boast of caging Hezekiah but never claim the city — a silence that matches the biblical account of a deliverance.

events.title: The fall of Nineveh
events.summary: Babylonians and Medes destroy the Assyrian capital. Nahum's oracle against Nineveh is about this collapse.

events.title: The Battle of Carchemish
events.summary: Nebuchadnezzar shatters Egypt and inherits the whole Levant. Judah passes overnight from the Egyptian sphere to the Babylonian, and the first deportation follows.

events.title: Jerusalem surrenders; Jehoiachin deported
events.summary: Babylon takes the city, deposes the king and deports the court and craftsmen — Ezekiel among them. Babylonian ration tablets listing Jehoiachin have been excavated.

events.title: The fall of Jerusalem
events.summary: After an eighteen-month siege the walls are breached, the temple burned and the population deported. The single most consequential event in the Old Testament.

events.title: Cyrus takes Babylon
events.summary: Persia takes the city with little fighting. The Cyrus Cylinder records his policy of sending deported peoples home to rebuild their sanctuaries.

events.title: The edict of Cyrus
events.summary: Exiles are permitted to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple. The first group goes home after roughly fifty years away.

events.title: The second temple is finished
events.summary: Twenty years after the return, and seventy after the destruction, the rebuilt temple is dedicated — smaller than Solomon's, and remembered as a disappointment by those who had seen the first.

events.title: The Battle of Marathon
events.summary: Athens defeats a Persian expedition. Persia's long failure in Greece begins here, and with it the shift of power westward.

events.title: Nehemiah rebuilds the walls
events.summary: The Persian king's cupbearer returns and refortifies Jerusalem in fifty-two days against local opposition.

events.title: Alexander conquers the Persian empire
events.summary: In three battles the Persian empire falls. Judea passes to Greek rule, and Greek becomes the common language — which is why the New Testament is written in it.

events.title: The Septuagint is begun
events.summary: The Hebrew scriptures are translated into Greek at Alexandria. Most Old Testament quotations in the New Testament follow this version.

events.title: Antiochus IV desecrates the temple
events.summary: Jewish practice is outlawed and a pagan altar set up in the temple. This is the 'abomination that causes desolation' the Gospels later echo.

events.title: The Maccabean revolt and rededication
events.summary: Priestly resistance retakes Jerusalem and purifies the temple, remembered as Hanukkah. Judea wins about a century of independence.

events.title: Pompey takes Jerusalem
events.summary: Rome ends Jewish independence and enters the holy of holies. Judea becomes a client state, and the Roman occupation of the Gospels begins here.

events.title: The Battle of Actium
events.summary: Octavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra and becomes sole master of the Roman world. The civil wars end and the empire begins.

events.title: Herod begins rebuilding the temple
events.summary: A vast reconstruction that ran for decades — the temple the disciples admired, finished only a few years before its destruction.

events.title: Judea comes under direct Roman rule
events.summary: Archelaus is deposed and Judea is governed by Roman prefects, with a census that triggers a revolt. This is why a Roman official, not a Jewish king, tries Jesus.

events.title: The crucifixion
events.summary: Under Tiberius, with Pilate as prefect and Caiaphas as high priest. Dated by most to AD 30 or 33.

events.title: Caligula orders his statue for the temple
events.summary: The emperor demands his image be installed in the temple. Only his assassination prevents it — a crisis that shaped Jewish expectations of Roman sacrilege.

events.title: Claudius expels the Jews from Rome
events.summary: Roman Jews are expelled after disturbances. Aquila and Priscilla arrive in Corinth as a result, which is how Paul meets them.

events.title: The fire of Rome
events.summary: Nero blames Christians for the fire and executes them publicly. The first state persecution; tradition places the deaths of Peter and Paul near this.

events.title: The Jewish revolt against Rome
events.summary: Revolt breaks out and Rome sends legions. Four years of war that end the world the Gospels describe.

events.title: The destruction of the temple
events.summary: Titus takes Jerusalem and burns the temple. Sacrificial worship ends permanently, and both Judaism and Christianity are reshaped by its absence.

events.title: The fall of Masada
events.summary: The last fortress holds out against a Roman siege ramp. The revolt is over.

events.title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii
events.summary: The eruption preserves a Roman town intact, giving the clearest picture we have of ordinary life in the world the epistles were written into.

backgrounds.title: Before the records begin
backgrounds.body: No external documents reach this far back, so there is no ruler or dated event to set beside these chapters. What does exist is a body of Mesopotamian literature covering the same ground: the Enuma Elish on the ordering of the world, the Atrahasis epic and the eleventh tablet of Gilgamesh on a flood survived in a boat, and king lists giving enormous lifespans to rulers before it. The similarities are close enough to show a shared stock of tradition, and the differences — one God rather than a quarrelling pantheon, a flood sent for moral reasons rather than because humans were noisy — are where the biblical account is making its argument.

backgrounds.title: A world of city-states and migrations
backgrounds.body: The patriarchal stories are set in a world with no single dominant power in Canaan. Mesopotamia is a patchwork of city-states; Egypt is strong but inward-looking; the land between them is a corridor of small towns and open country where herding families can move with their flocks. That is exactly the world the narratives assume — Abraham can travel from Ur to Harran to Canaan to Egypt and back without crossing a guarded frontier, and can negotiate for a burial plot with local townsmen as an outsider with standing but no land.

backgrounds.title: Egypt at the height of its empire
backgrounds.body: New Kingdom Egypt was the superpower of its day, and Canaan was its province. Egyptian garrisons held the coast road, local kings sent tribute and hostages, and pharaoh's court kept an anxious correspondence with city rulers who feared their neighbours more than they feared Egypt. Enormous building projects ran on conscripted labour, and Semitic-speaking populations lived in the eastern delta. An exodus from Egypt was therefore not an escape from one city, but an escape from the reach of an empire that also controlled the land being escaped to.

backgrounds.title: The empires withdraw
backgrounds.body: Around 1200 BC the eastern Mediterranean fell apart. The Hittite empire vanished, trade routes closed, cities burned, and Egypt pulled back to its own borders. Into that vacuum came new peoples — among them the Philistines on the coast — and it was in the same vacuum that highland villages in Canaan multiplied without an empire to stop them. The book of Judges describes precisely this: no central authority anywhere, local strongmen rising and falling, and repeated pressure from better-armed neighbours on the plains.

backgrounds.title: A window with no superpower
backgrounds.body: The united monarchy occupies a rare gap in ancient history: Egypt was weak, Assyria had not yet risen, and no great power was pressing on the Levant. That is what made a modest local kingdom possible at all — the trade routes between Egypt and Mesopotamia ran through territory nobody larger was holding, and control of them made a small state rich. When Assyria recovered in the next century, that window closed and never reopened.

backgrounds.title: Assyria arrives
backgrounds.body: The dominant fact of this era is the rise of Assyria: a military state that turned conquest into administration, replacing local dynasties with provinces and deporting whole populations to break their identity. Israel and Judah became small players choosing sides — pay tribute, or join a coalition and risk annihilation. Almost every prophetic warning about foreign alliances in this period is a warning about that choice, and the Assyrian records themselves name Israelite kings paying up.

backgrounds.title: One kingdom left
backgrounds.body: After Samaria fell in 722, Judah survived alone for another one hundred and thirty-six years, wedged between Assyria, Egypt and later Babylon. Its kings' central problem was which empire to appease. Hezekiah gambled on rebellion and nearly lost Jerusalem; Josiah tried to exploit Assyria's collapse and was killed by Egypt at Megiddo. The prophets of this period speak into a state whose survival was permanently in question.

backgrounds.title: Life after the temple
backgrounds.body: Babylon deported Judah's elite in stages and destroyed the temple in 586. What followed was not slavery but resettlement: exiles held land, wrote letters, ran businesses, and some rose at court. The crisis was theological rather than material. Worship had been centred on one building that no longer existed, in a land they no longer held, under a god who appeared to have lost. The response — scripture collected and studied, sabbath and circumcision as portable identity, prophecy reaching beyond national restoration — reshaped the faith permanently.

backgrounds.title: Under Persia, then Greece, then Rome
backgrounds.body: The return home did not mean independence. Judea spent this era as a small province passed between empires: Persian for two centuries, Greek after Alexander, contested between Ptolemies and Seleucids, briefly independent under the Hasmoneans after the Maccabean revolt, then Roman from 63 BC. Each rule left something behind — Persian administrative structures, the Greek language and the Septuagint, a hardened resistance to religious interference, and finally a Roman occupation. The world of the Gospels is the sediment of all four.

backgrounds.title: The Roman peace, and its price
backgrounds.body: Augustus ended a century of civil war and built a system that held the Mediterranean together: roads, sea lanes, one currency, a common Greek tongue for trade. It also ran on taxation collected by contractors, on crucifixion as public deterrence, and on emperors who accepted divine honours. The same network that made a provincial preacher's execution routine is the network that carried news of it to Rome within a generation.

backgrounds.title: Occupied Judea
backgrounds.body: Herod the Great ruled as Rome's client king, hated and monumentally effective. At his death his territory split between his sons, and Judea itself passed to Roman prefects within a decade, with the high priesthood appointed and deposed at Roman pleasure. This is why authority in the Gospels is fragmented: a Roman prefect who alone could execute, a Herodian tetrarch over Galilee, a temple aristocracy managing a compromise, Pharisees with religious influence but no power, and revolutionary movements waiting in the hills. Luke names four of these five in a single sentence when he dates John the Baptist's ministry.

backgrounds.title: A movement inside an empire
backgrounds.body: The church spread along Roman infrastructure — the roads, the ports, the Jewish communities already established in every major city. Rome was initially indifferent, treating the movement as a Jewish sect and therefore legally tolerated. That changed under Nero, and by Domitian's insistence on divine titles the conflict was structural: an empire whose unity ran through the emperor's honours met a movement that would not give them. The letters of the New Testament are written into that narrowing space.

backgrounds.title: The war that ended the world of the Gospels
backgrounds.body: Revolt broke out in 66, and by 70 Jerusalem and the temple were gone. Sacrificial worship stopped permanently, the priestly aristocracy vanished with it, and both surviving movements — rabbinic Judaism and the church — became religions of text and assembly rather than temple. Nearly everything written in the New Testament after this point is written on the far side of that break, and much written before it reads differently once you know it was coming.
